prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

It is important to note that the perceived level of safety, does not necessarily correspond to the actual level of safety (Cho et al., 2009), and that road users might compensate for a higher level of perceived safety, by showing riskier behavior (Wilde, 1982). In this study, only the perceptions of road users were investigated, which does not allow a direct transfer to actual behavior. For road users’ perceptions of increased safety of road crossings on the 3D crosswalk in comparison to traditional crosswalks, there are a number of potential reasons. Unrelated to the 3D effect of the crosswalk, road users could perceive the painted area of the 3D crosswalk as larger compared to traditional crosswalks. The drawing pattern used to produce the optical illusion of the 3D crosswalk (Fig. 2) breaks apart the straight lines that make up a traditional crosswalk, which could lead to a perceived increase of the painted area, and thereby the perceived visibility of the 3D crosswalk. Related to this, road users might compare the visibility of the newly painted 3D crosswalk to the average visibility of older traditional crosswalks that they encounter in the road system. As the majority of traditional crosswalks that road users encounter will be considerably older than the 3D crosswalk, their paint will have faded more, potentially decreasing objective as well as perceived visibility of traditional crosswalks in comparison to the new 3D crosswalk. Increased safety perceptions due to a perceived larger painted area and higher color intensity of the 3D crosswalk would be in line with research that shows a relation between the visibility of a crosswalk and pedestrian safety (Feldman, Manzi, & Mitman, 2010; Fitz- patrick, Chrysler, Iragavarapu, & Park, 2011; Guo, & Boyle, 2022; Pulugurtha, Vasudevan, Nambisan, & Dangeti, 2012; Sarwar et al., 219 F.W. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

In this study, only the perceptions of road users were investigated, which does not allow a direct transfer to actual behavior. For road users’ perceptions of increased safety of road crossings on the 3D crosswalk in comparison to traditional crosswalks, there are a number of potential reasons. Unrelated to the 3D effect of the crosswalk, road users could perceive the painted area of the 3D crosswalk as larger compared to traditional crosswalks. The drawing pattern used to produce the optical illusion of the 3D crosswalk (Fig. 2) breaks apart the straight lines that make up a traditional crosswalk, which could lead to a perceived increase of the painted area, and thereby the perceived visibility of the 3D crosswalk. Related to this, road users might compare the visibility of the newly painted 3D crosswalk to the average visibility of older traditional crosswalks that they encounter in the road system. As the majority of traditional crosswalks that road users encounter will be considerably older than the 3D crosswalk, their paint will have faded more, potentially decreasing objective as well as perceived visibility of traditional crosswalks in comparison to the new 3D crosswalk. Increased safety perceptions due to a perceived larger painted area and higher color intensity of the 3D crosswalk would be in line with research that shows a relation between the visibility of a crosswalk and pedestrian safety (Feldman, Manzi, & Mitman, 2010; Fitz- patrick, Chrysler, Iragavarapu, & Park, 2011; Guo, & Boyle, 2022; Pulugurtha, Vasudevan, Nambisan, & Dangeti, 2012; Sarwar et al., 219 F.W. Discussion Many studies show, in other contexts, that youth display safer behavior than seniors (Herrero-Fern´andez etal., 2016). Among the factors associated with this difference are several concerning structural and subjective individual conditions (cognitive ability, education level, attitudes, perception of control of their behavior), other physical con- ditions related to crossing (length of the crossing, topography), and other environmental factors (climate, signage, and physical crossing conditions). Herein, it was found that age could be less critical in risky crossing behavior. The pedestrian profile model showed that the dimension related to road safety education and sex, Cronbach’s alpha 0.67, had a more significant influence than age on risky behavior.
